data.copy:
I used to think dog training was about willpower.
 
The dog's willpower. My willpower. Whether I was consistent enough, patient enough, firm enough. Whether the dog was smart enough, stubborn enough, motivated enough.
 
After two years of dealing with my dog Max and his barking, and after buying what I can only describe as an embarrassing collection of devices and programs that did nothing useful, I learned that I had been thinking about this completely wrong.
 
If you have bought a device that worked for ten days and then stopped working, this is for you. If you have had a trainer tell you your dog needs months of consistency while your neighbor is filing complaints this week, this is for you. If you have stood in a pet store aisle reading box descriptions and suspected that none of them were going to work, you were right, and I want to explain exactly why.
 
Max is a four-year-old Belgian Malinois mix. If you know the breed, you already understand the baseline energy level. If you do not know the breed, imagine a dog that was designed by someone who thought German Shepherds were a little too relaxed.
 
He is brilliant and loyal and completely impossible to settle down when something catches his attention. And when Max decided something was worth barking at, which was everything that moved within range of our fence, he committed. Long sustained bursts. Not the two barks and done that you read about in dog training articles. Full episodes that could go five, ten minutes before whatever triggered him moved out of range.
 
I am a person who works from home. I have a client that pays me for clear audio on regular calls. I have neighbors who have been patient for two years and were starting to run out of patience. And I have a dog who I love and did not want to live in conflict with.
 
I tried the obvious things first.
 
Dog behavior is not about willpower. It is about biology.

data.copy:
My Dog's Chronic Itching Story: How I Finally Found Relief After 18 Months of Hell

By Jennifer Mitchell

If you're reading this at 2 AM listening to your dog scratch themselves bloody... I see you. I was you.

For 18 months, I lived in what I can only describe as pet owner hell. My dog Cooper's skin looked like someone was torturing him every single night.

The worst part? Three different vets looked at his allergy panels and said the same thing: "His tests are normal. This is just atopic dermatitis. Here's Apoquel."

But if his allergies were "normal," then why was his skin getting worse every night? Why did Apoquel make him lethargic without touching the itching?

Nothing made sense.

Let me back up and tell you my whole story, because if you're going through this right now, you need to hear it...

==== When It Started ====

Cooper is 6 years old. Two years ago, I started noticing him licking his paws after walks. Nothing major at first – just annoying.

But within 3 months, that paw licking became constant. Raw, bleeding skin that made me want to cry every time I looked at his paws.

I'd wake up at 2 AM every single night to the sound of scratching. My husband started sleeping in the guest room because the noise kept him awake.

Cooper couldn't lie on his bed without scratching. He couldn't walk on our hardwood floors without leaving bloody paw prints. I had to keep him in a cone 24/7 just to prevent him from making it worse.

It was heartbreaking.

Vet #1: "His allergy panel looks normal. Here's Apoquel."

Vet #2: "This is common in Golden Retrievers. You'll have to manage it."

I spent $4,200+ on specialists, Apoquel, Cytopoint injections, medicated shampoos, special diets, air purifiers. NOTHING worked.

The Apoquel made him tired and depressed. He'd just lie there all day. My daughter said he seemed "drugged" all the time.

My wife paid a lawyer three hundred dollars to start our divorce before anybody found out what was actually wrong with her.

She told me afterwards that she wasn't leaving me. She was leaving what she thought she'd turned into.

I'm Mark, I'm 47, and I live in Cincinnati with my wife Claire and our two kids — Ellie who's fourteen and Sam who's eleven.

I'm writing this for any man who has quietly started thinking his wife has changed, or lost interest, or just stopped trying. And for any woman who has already decided on her own that her family would be better off without her, because something is wrong with her body and every single person she's asked has told her she's fine.

It took us nearly two years to get an answer, and the answer came off the back of an envelope at our kitchen table, not from any of the six people we paid.

Claire is 45. She swam competitively in high school, she ran the Flying Pig half marathon twice, she was the one still talking in the kitchen at one in the morning when everyone else had gone home. When we first started dating she used to give me a hard time for wanting to go to bed before midnight.

It came on so slowly that neither of us ever pointed at a day and said that's when it started.

The tiredness was first. Not worn out after a long week. Empty. She'd sleep nine hours on a Saturday, come downstairs at ten thirty still in her robe, sit on the arm of the couch and say she felt like she'd been drugged. By fall she was going up to bed at eight o'clock, before Sam. Exhausted. Eyes barely open. Nine hours of sleep and still waking up like she hadn't slept at all.

Then even the sleep stopped working.

Sometime around January she started waking up at two in the morning — sheets soaked, heart pounding, heat rolling through her body in waves that came out of nowhere. Three, four times a night. data.copy:
"Maybe you just have to use poison."

Seven words from my wife that nearly broke me. Not because she was being cruel. But because after six months of fighting mice, a $5,800 exterminator quote, and a 4:30am moment with my dog I'll never forget, I was starting to wonder if she was right.

It started last October, the way it always does. A few droppings in the pantry. A chewed corner on a bag of birdseed. Then a small gray flash along the baseboard while I made my coffee.

I'm 67. I spent 35 years as an electrician before I retired. I live in an older home in Ohio with my wife and Duke, our 9-year-old lab. I've fixed my own roof, rewired my own basement, and I don't scare easy. But before there was even a real problem, I'd already decided there were certain things I would not do.

I would not use poison. Not with Duke sleeping six feet from where I'd set it. My neighbor lost his terrier two years ago to a mouse that had eaten rodenticide out in the field. I'd read enough about secondary poisoning to know that even if Duke never found the bait, he could find the mouse.

So I did everything a responsible, careful pet owner is supposed to do.

Live-catch traps. The little plastic boxes with the trap door. I caught a mouse the first night, drove him a mile down the road, and let him go at dawn feeling pretty good about myself. Three days later, fresh droppings on the counter. My buddy Gary finally said it for me. "You're not solving anything. You're just commuting."

Snap traps. Caught a few, then nothing for weeks. The mice learned the trigger and stole the bait without setting it off. I watched peanut butter vanish overnight while the bar stayed loaded.

Single-frequency ultrasonic plug-ins. Eighty dollars. Duke ignored them. So did the mice.

data.copy:
There's a version of this story where I never find out, where everything just keeps going the way it was going, and honestly that possibility still keeps me up at night.

His name is Milo.

He's an orange tabby with one white paw and this habit of sitting on the bathroom counter every single morning while I brush my teeth, just staring at me in the mirror like he's supervising. He's been doing that for seven years.

When I first got him, I was in a place I don't talk about much. My mom had just passed after a long, awful fight with cancer, and I was dealing with anxiety so bad I couldn't sleep through the night.

I'd wake up at 3am with my chest tight and my mind racing, convinced something terrible was about to happen, unable to turn it off.

A friend suggested I foster a cat. Just to have something else in the apartment. Something warm and alive.

Milo showed up in a carrier, skinny and skittish, and the rescue said he'd been returned twice because he was "too needy."

He wasn't needy. He just wanted to be close.

That first night, he climbed onto my chest while I was lying in bed staring at the ceiling, and he stayed there. Purring. Just this steady, warm weight right over my heart.

And I fell asleep. For the first time in weeks, I fell asleep.

After that, he did it every night. He'd wait until I was lying down, then he'd climb up, settle in, and purr until I drifted off.

On the mornings I didn't want to get out of bed — and there were a lot of them — he'd sit on my chest and headbutt my chin until I got up to feed him.

He didn't know he was saving me. He just was.

I kept him, obviously. I couldn't imagine my life without him.

Over the years, he became this constant. My alarm clock. My shadow. The reason I came home at a decent hour instead of staying late at work.

He had this weird thing where he'd steal hair ties off the bathroom counter and leave them in his food bowl. I have no idea why. I stopped questioning it.

To anyone who has woken up to find blood on their sheets from a seborrheic keratosis they scratched off in their sleep — after spending hundreds trying to keep them under control — this is why nothing you've tried was ever going to get ahead of what your skin keeps producing.

I've always known which ones itch worse than others.

The ones along my back and shoulder blades, mostly. I'd lie there some nights running my finger across them in the dark, trying to work out if it was worse than the night before or about the same.

I have a lot of these. Like — a lot. Flat cornflake-ish ones. Harder warty ones, the kind that catch under my fingernail if I'm not careful.

Scratching without meaning to. Waking up having scratched in my sleep more times than I could count.

The first time I found a little blood on my sheets, I assumed I'd nicked myself shaving, or scratched an ordinary itch too hard. Small spot. Didn't think much of it.

It kept happening. Every few weeks, a small mark on the sheet or my nightshirt, always somewhere near my shoulder or my back.

I started checking before I even got up some mornings. Running my hand along the spots I knew were the worst, feeling for anything raw or tender before I looked at the sheets properly.

Some mornings, nothing. Some mornings, I already knew what I'd find before I found it.

I just wanted to stop waking up to evidence of something I couldn't even feel happening.

I just didn't know yet that there was something that could actually change that.

I knew something had to change the morning I woke up and the blood had gone through my nightshirt onto the sheet underneath it.

Not a small mark this time. Enough that I had to change the sheets before I'd even had coffee.

I found the spot — one along my shoulder blade, raw, the surface torn away. I hadn't felt it happen. I never do.

data.caption: kittysupps.com
data.copy:
The advice I gave cat owners for 14 years was making their cats sicker.

I found out when it happened to mine.

I'm a veterinarian. When Theo started throwing up his meals — I knew exactly what to do.

Switch to pate. Switch proteins. Sensitive stomach formula.

I did all of it.

He kept throwing up.

And I finally understood what every frustrated owner had been trying to tell me.

The advice was never going to work.

Because I had been prescribing the wrong solution for the wrong problem for 14 years.

My name is Sienna Rose. I've been a vet for fourteen years.

And I just admitted something I should have seen a long time ago: almost everything I told owners about a cat who keeps throwing up was wrong.

This is hard to write.

For over a decade, I told every owner with a vomiting cat the same things.

It's probably the food. Switch him to a wet pate — it's gentler, easier to digest.

If he still brings it up, try a different brand. Switch proteins; maybe he's reacting to the chicken.

Try the sensitive-stomach formula. The prescription cans. And give it time.

Standard advice. Exactly what I was trained to say.

Then a little over a year ago, my own cat — Theo — started throwing up his meals.

Not hairballs. Food. An hour after he ate, in a long, undigested tube on the floor. Some mornings, yellow foam before I'd even had my coffee.

Annoying, but fixable, I told myself. So I did exactly what I'd been telling owners to do for years.

I switched him to a soft, premium pate. Everyone swears it's gentler.

He threw it up too — only now, instead of right after eating, it came back about an hour later, in that perfect meat-tube shape. Whole. Untouched. Like it had never been digested at all.

So I switched brands. Fancy Feast to Tiki Cat to Weruva. I switched proteins — chicken to salmon to turkey.

I bought the sensitive-stomach formula. The hydrolyzed prescription diet my own clinic sells, sixty-eight dollars a case.

Still throwing up. Most days. Sometime…

The Muslim student in my Hermeneutics class never seemed to study, never raised her hand for attention, and barely spoke unless the professor called on her.

But every single time he did call on her, she’d answer the question better than the rest of us combined. When I finally asked her how she did it, her secret had nothing to do with how smart she was.

I went to a small college in the South, and Hermeneutics was the class everyone dreaded.

It’s the study of how to interpret Scripture. Context, original languages, literary genres, historical background. The kind of class that separates people who think they understand the Bible from people who actually do.

Our class had 12 students. All of us except one had been raised in the faith since childhood. A few were already serving in ministry. And every single one of us walked into that first class assuming we’d do well.

We were wrong.

The professor would ask a question about a passage, and the room would go quiet. We’d fumble through answers, guess at meanings, share opinions we couldn't back up. He’d patiently correct us, and we’d write down what he said and move on.

And then there was Layla.

Layla Karim. Barely 22 years old. Quiet. Always sat in the back row, wearing a soft gray hijab. Never raised her hand for the easy questions. Never tried to sound impressive.

But every single time the professor called on her, she answered like she’d already studied the passage for a week. And what made it even more remarkable was that she was not a Christian. She had told the professor on the first day of class that she was Muslim, that she had grown up memorizing the Quran in Arabic, and that she had enrolled in the class out of curiosity about the faith of the community she had been living inside her entire life. data.caption: Mom Lost Her Teeth at 69. I Started Doing The Same Thing ☹
data.copy:
I am going to say something that nobody with receding gums wants to hear and I don't care if it upsets you.

Switching to a different toothpaste is not going to save your gums.

Not Sensodyne. Not Parodontax. Not the prescription fluoride gel your dentist just handed you.

NONE OF IT IS GOING TO WORK.

I know because I watched my mother go through all of it. Every brand. Every "gum repair" formula. Every "clinically proven" mouthwash. For eleven years. And she lost six teeth anyway. 69 years old. Two rounds of painful deep cleaning. A gum graft that partially failed. Because she spent eleven years treating a SURFACE problem that was never a surface problem.

And the worst part? I started down the exact same road. Same pink in the sink every morning. Same teeth that looked a little longer every month. Same slow, creeping dread every time I ran my tongue along my gum line.

And I almost let it happen to me because I was still following the same advice that destroyed my mother's smile.

I'm done being polite about this. If your gums are still pulling back and you're in here asking which toothpaste to switch to next, you are wasting time your gums do not have.

Read this entire post. Every word. Because the answer is in here and it is NOT another tube of toothpaste or another bottle of mouthwash.

My name is Diane. I'm 53. I live in Nashville with my husband Paul.

My mother passed away fourteen months ago. She was 69.

She didn't die from the gum disease. But the last decade of her life — every dinner, every family photo, every time someone handed her a cold glass of water — was shaped by it.
